description: Common chicory (Cichorium intybus) is a somewhat woody, perennial herbaceous plant of the dandelion family Asteraceae, usually with bright blue flowers, rarely white or pink.

growing_information.text:
Chicory is grown for two or three purposes. The root of this plant is the common adulterant of coffee, and large quantities are used for this purpose. The commercial growing of chicory is con [65] fined to a few sections, as the crop will not thrive on every kind of soil. A deep, rich loam, without excessive amounts of clay or sand, is desirable, and soil that is not too rich in nitrogenous matter is best suited to the production of roots. The roots are frequently placed in soil under a greenhouse bench or in a warm cellar and covered with a foot or more of straw, or with a light covering of straw and then several inches of warm manure. Under this covering the leaves will be formed in a solid head, which is known on the market as witloof. Chicory has run wild in some parts of the country and is considered a bad weed.

The handsome blue flowers, which are borne the second season, are very attractive. As a pot herb chicory is used like spinach, but the leaves should be boiled in two waters to remove the bitter taste. As a salad the roots are dug in the autumn and planted in cellars or under a greenhouse bench, where they produce an abundance of blanched leaves, which are eaten raw. The blanched leaves are also boiled and used as greens.—(F.B. 255; U. Idaho E. S. 10.)

growing_information.text: Chicory has various uses and is now quite largely grown in gardens. As a salad plant only the tender, blanched leaves of the crown are used. The outer, green leaves are often used for “greens,” like dandelion. Chicory is not a surface feeder like most salad plants, but is grown as a root crop the same as carrots or parsnips. The soil must be deep, that the roots may come to perfection by fall; cuttings of leaves may be made during the season. The roots may be left in the ground over the winter. Chicory is really a perennial, but under cultivation [146] it is better to grow a new lot of plants each year. When wanted for winter use, the strong roots are taken up in the fall, and buried in a sloping direction in a pit or cellar, with the crown of the plant showing an inch or so above the sand or earth. The growing-place must be kept dark, and in a few weeks the small, prized leaves begin to show. When chicory plants are covered, crowns and all, with about two feet of manure, they develop heads resembling lettuce heads. The young, tender roots of chicory are eaten as beets or carrots are, while the dried root is extensively used in place of coffee. This accounts for the increased area devoted to chicory in this country of recent years; it is less injurious to the nerves than coffee.

Chicory is a versatile plant grown for its roots, which are used as a coffee substitute, and for its tender leaves, which can be eaten raw in salads or cooked like greens. To grow chicory successfully, choose a deep, rich loam soil that is not excessively clayey or sandy and has moderate nitrogen content. Chicory roots require ample depth to develop fully by fall. Plant chicory seeds directly into the garden in early spring, spacing them about 6-8 inches apart in rows that are 12-15 inches apart. The plants can be left in the ground over winter if desired. For winter use, dig up the strong roots in the fall and bury them in a pit or cellar at a sloping angle, with the crown of the plant showing about an inch above the sand or earth. Keep the growing area dark; within a few weeks, small, tender leaves will begin to emerge. Alternatively, cover the plants with about two feet of manure to develop heads resembling lettuce. Chicory is considered a perennial but is typically grown as an annual for better control over plant health and yield. The young, tender roots can be eaten like beets or carrots. Chicory has attractive blue flowers in its second season but can become weedy if not managed properly.
